question: A 10-year-old child presents two weeks after untreated sore throat with migratory large-joint pain, fever 102°F, and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex. Which combination of findings from the Revised Jones Criteria would establish the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever?
cited_learning_objective: Know the Revised Jones Criteria – Major/Minor for Diagnosis

options.rationale: Correct: Two Major manifestations (migratory arthritis and carditis) meet the Revised Jones requirement when GAS evidence is present.
Wrong: These are two Minor criteria; diagnosis requires two Major or one Major plus two Minor. Would be correct only with an additional Major.
Wrong: One Major (erythema marginatum) plus one Minor (prolonged PR) is insufficient; would need one more Minor to be diagnostic.
Wrong: One Major (subcutaneous nodules) plus one Minor (arthralgia) is insufficient; needs an additional Minor to meet criteria.
Wrong: Chorea can be a sole Major for presumptive diagnosis, but only when accompanied by evidence of preceding GAS infection; without GAS evidence it is insufficient.

question: Which laboratory test provides direct evidence of a recent group A streptococcal infection required by the Revised Jones Criteria?
cited_learning_objective: Know the Revised Jones Criteria – Major/Minor for Diagnosis

options.rationale: Correct: A positive throat culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is listed as evidence of preceding GAS infection.
Wrong: Elevated ESR is a Minor criterion and not direct evidence of GAS; it would not substitute for microbiologic proof.
Wrong: A normal ASO titer does not indicate recent GAS infection; a rising or elevated titer would be required.
Wrong: Blood cultures are not the standard evidence for preceding pharyngitis in the criteria; throat culture or rising ASO/ADB titers are specified.
Wrong: Influenza testing is unrelated to GAS infection and would not satisfy the Jones requirement.

question: Which of the following is a Major manifestation in the Revised Jones Criteria?
cited_learning_objective: Know the Revised Jones Criteria – Major/Minor for Diagnosis

options.rationale: Correct: Erythema marginatum is explicitly listed as a Major manifestation in the Revised Jones Criteria.
Wrong: Fever is a Minor manifestation; only high fever contributes as a Minor criterion, not a Major.
Wrong: Arthralgia is a Minor manifestation; migratory arthritis with objective joint findings is Major.
Wrong: Prolonged PR interval is a Minor criterion; QT prolongation is not part of the criteria.
Wrong: Elevated rheumatoid factor is a nonspecific lab finding in ARF but not a Major manifestation in the Jones Criteria.

question: Which statement about the epidemiology of rheumatic heart disease is supported by the material?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: RHD remains common in developing countries
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state RHD remains a major cause of cardiovascular disease in developing countries and is linked to poverty and limited access to care.

options.text: RHD incidence is rising in industrialized nations
options.rationale: Wrong: The material reports a sharp decline in industrialized countries due to treatment of GAS pharyngitis; rising incidence would contradict the slide.
Wrong: ARF most frequently occurs in children 5–15 years; RHD follows years later, not primarily in older adults as initial disease.

options.text: RHD causes less than 1% of heart failure worldwide
options.rationale: Wrong: The slides note in developing countries RHD accounts for about 15% of heart failure, so  12 months after surgery and is more often due to organisms like Strep or HACEK; 6 months is early.
Wrong: The patient has a prosthetic valve and timing fits early PVE, not native valve disease.
Wrong: The prosthetic aortic valve is left-sided; right-sided IE refers to tricuspid/pulmonary valve involvement.
Wrong: Fungal PVE is possible but the organism here is coagulase-negative staphylococci, a bacterial cause, so fungal categorization is incorrect.

question: Which echocardiographic approach should be performed first when infective endocarditis is suspected, per the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides recommend initial TTE, with TEE if TTE is nondiagnostic or higher-risk organisms are suspected.
Wrong: TEE is more sensitive but the material advises starting with TTE and proceeding to TEE as needed.
Wrong: Cardiac MRI is not listed as the initial imaging modality; echocardiography (TTE/TEE) is recommended first.
Wrong: Chest x-ray may show complications but cannot replace echocardiography for diagnosing valvular vegetations.

options.text: No imaging if blood cultures positive
options.rationale: Wrong: Positive cultures do not obviate imaging; echocardiography is still required to assess vegetations and complications.

question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis has persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antibiotics for 8 days. According to the surgical indications in the material, what is the recommended next consideration?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: Persistence of bacteremia >1 week on appropriate antibiotics is listed as an indication to consider surgery.
Wrong: Ongoing bacteremia despite appropriate therapy suggests need for surgical evaluation rather than indefinite continuation alone.
Wrong: Oral therapy is not recommended for persistent bacteremia; slides emphasize prolonged IV bactericidal therapy and surgical consideration.

options.text: Stop antibiotics and repeat cultures later
options.rationale: Wrong: Stopping antibiotics would risk worsening infection; persistent bacteremia requires escalation, not cessation.
Wrong: Antifungals are indicated only for fungal IE; persistent bacterial bacteremia does not warrant empiric antifungal therapy.

question: Which of the following cardiac conditions is listed among the highest risk for requiring infective endocarditis prophylaxis before certain procedures?
cited_learning_objective: Given a patient scenario, identify a patient requiring antibiotic prophylaxis against infectious endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides list prosthetic heart valves as a highest-risk condition warranting prophylaxis for qualifying procedures.
Wrong: MVP without regurgitation is not listed as a high-risk condition; prophylaxis is generally not indicated for it.
Wrong: CABG alone is not listed as a high-risk condition requiring lifelong prophylaxis in the slides.
Wrong: While some congenital defects are high risk, the slides emphasize unrepaired cyanotic CHD and prosthetic material; an isolated small VSD is not listed as highest risk.
Wrong: HCM without prosthetic material or prior IE is not among the highest-risk categories in the material.

question: A patient with a history of prior infective endocarditis is scheduled for a dental extraction. According to the slides, should antibiotic prophylaxis be given?
cited_learning_objective: Given a patient scenario, identify a patient requiring antibiotic prophylaxis against infectious endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: Prior history of IE is listed among the highest-risk conditions for which prophylaxis is recommended for dental procedures involving mucosal manipulation.
Wrong: The slides specify that patients with prior IE are high risk and should receive prophylaxis for qualifying procedures.
Wrong: Prior IE alone is sufficient to warrant prophylaxis; prosthetic valve is an additional high-risk condition but not required here.
Wrong: Prophylaxis is recommended for dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or perforate oral mucosa, including extractions, not limited to scaling.

options.text: Only if blood cultures positive preop
options.rationale: Wrong: Prophylaxis decisions are based on risk category and procedure, not on preoperative blood culture status.

question: Which dental antibiotic regimen is listed as the first-line prophylactic choice in the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Given a patient scenario, identify a patient requiring antibiotic prophylaxis against infectious endocarditis

options.text: Amoxicillin 2 g PO one hour before
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state the recommended regimen is 2 g of amoxicillin PO one hour before the procedure.

options.text: Clindamycin 600 mg PO one hour before
options.rationale: Wrong: Clindamycin is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients but is not listed as first-line in the slides.

options.text: Erythromycin 1 g PO one hour before
options.rationale: Wrong: Erythromycin is no longer recommended by the AHA per the slides and is not first-line.

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg PO two hours before
options.rationale: Wrong: The slides list doxycycline dosing as 100 mg but do not present it as first-line; timing and indication differ from amoxicillin.

options.text: Azithromycin 500 mg PO one hour before
options.rationale: Wrong: Azithromycin is an alternative for penicillin allergy but is not the first-line agent listed in the slides.

question: A 12-year-old with acute rheumatic fever is treated for carditis. According to the slides, which anti-inflammatory agent and dosing range is recommended for children?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.rationale: Correct: The slides recommend aspirin 80–100 mg/kg/day in children for carditis and arthritis in ARF.
Wrong: The slides specify aspirin dosing for ARF carditis; ibuprofen dosing is not provided as the recommended therapy.
Wrong: Steroids are not listed as first-line anti-inflammatory therapy for ARF carditis in the slides; aspirin is recommended.
Wrong: Acetaminophen treats fever and pain but is not the anti-inflammatory agent recommended for ARF carditis.
Wrong: Colchicine is not mentioned in the slides as treatment for ARF carditis or arthritis.

question: Which late valvular lesion is described as the most common long-term consequence of rheumatic heart disease in the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.rationale: Correct: The slides state mitral stenosis due to leaflet fusion and calcification is the most common chronic lesion from RHD.
Wrong: Tricuspid disease is less commonly the primary chronic lesion; mitral involvement is most common per the slides.
Wrong: Pulmonary valve disease is not highlighted as a common sequela of RHD in the material.

options.text: Aortic stenosis from congenital bicuspid valve
options.rationale: Wrong: Aortic stenosis can occur but the slides emphasize mitral stenosis as the most common RHD lesion; congenital bicuspid etiology is separate.
Wrong: Mitral prolapse is not described as the typical chronic outcome of rheumatic valvulitis; stenosis and regurgitation are emphasized.

question: A patient with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis develops atrial fibrillation. According to the slides, what management step is specifically indicated to reduce embolic stroke risk?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.rationale: Correct: The slides state AF in mitral stenosis requires anticoagulation with warfarin to prevent embolic stroke.
Wrong: Valvuloplasty may be definitive therapy for severe MS but anticoagulation is the immediate step to reduce embolic risk; valvuloplasty alone would not address acute embolic prevention.
Wrong: Aspirin alone is insufficient for stroke prevention in AF with MS per the slides; warfarin anticoagulation is recommended.
Wrong: Rate control addresses symptoms but does not prevent embolic stroke; anticoagulation is required.
Wrong: Dual antiplatelet therapy is not the recommended stroke prevention strategy in AF with MS; warfarin anticoagulation is specified.

question: A 7-year-old with suspected ARF has choreiform movements as the only current manifestation and a history of sore throat one month ago. According to the slides, how should this presentation be interpreted regarding diagnosis?
cited_learning_objective: Know the Revised Jones Criteria – Major/Minor for Diagnosis

options.text: Presumptive ARF diagnosis with chorea alone
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state chorea can be the sole manifestation allowing a presumptive diagnosis of ARF in certain circumstances.

options.text: Cannot diagnose without two Major signs
options.rationale: Wrong: While two Major are usually required, chorea is an exception permitting presumptive diagnosis when it is the only manifestation.

options.text: Require positive blood cultures for GAS
options.rationale: Wrong: Blood cultures are not required; evidence of preceding GAS infection (throat culture or rising ASO/ADB) supports diagnosis but chorea alone can be presumptive.

options.text: Diagnosis only if subcutaneous nodules present
options.rationale: Wrong: Subcutaneous nodules are a Major but are not required when chorea is the sole manifestation per the slides.

options.text: Treat as viral chorea, not ARF
options.rationale: Wrong: Given recent GAS pharyngitis and chorea, ARF presumptive diagnosis is appropriate per the slides; labeling as viral would miss ARF.

question: A 60-year-old with prosthetic mitral valve presents with fever after dental extraction. Which procedural category from the slides would have indicated prophylaxis for this patient?
cited_learning_objective: Given a patient scenario, identify a patient requiring antibiotic prophylaxis against infectious endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides list dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or periapical region as qualifying for prophylaxis in high-risk patients like those with prosthetic valves.

options.text: Routine dental cleaning without tissue trauma
options.rationale: Wrong: Prophylaxis is indicated for procedures that manipulate gingiva or perforate mucosa; routine cleaning without trauma typically does not qualify.
Wrong: Radiography does not involve mucosal manipulation and would not require prophylaxis per the slides.
Wrong: Topical applications that do not perforate mucosa are not listed as indications for prophylaxis.
Wrong: The slides specify initial placement of orthodontic bands as a potential indication; routine bracket adjustments are not listed as qualifying procedures.

question: A patient with suspected left-sided native valve infective endocarditis has blood cultures growing Streptococcus viridans. According to the antibiotic guidance in the slides, which regimen is appropriate for this organism?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides list PCN G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin, as treatment options for Streptococcus viridans native valve IE.
Wrong: Nafcillin targets MSSA and is not the recommended primary therapy for viridans streptococci per the slides.
Wrong: Vancomycin is reserved for penicillin-allergic patients or resistant organisms; PCN G or ceftriaxone are preferred for viridans streptococci.
Wrong: Amphotericin B is for fungal IE; bacterial viridans infection is treated with beta-lactams, not antifungals.
Wrong: IE requires prolonged IV bactericidal therapy; oral amoxicillin outpatient is inadequate for native valve IE treatment.

question: A 45-year-old dialysis patient with a central venous catheter develops fever and positive blood cultures. The slides note certain infected devices usually require removal. Which device management is recommended for catheter-related infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.text: Remove the catheter and give antibiotics
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state dialysis grafts and central lines usually need removal in the setting of infection along with antibiotics.

options.text: Leave catheter and treat with oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong: Retaining an infected catheter and using oral antibiotics contradicts the slide guidance; removal plus IV therapy is recommended.

options.text: Replace catheter at same site immediately
options.rationale: Wrong: Immediate replacement at the same site risks persistent infection; slides recommend removal of infected hardware.
Wrong: Topical measures are insufficient for catheter-related bacteremia or endocarditis; systemic therapy and removal are required.
Wrong: Antibiotics should be started after obtaining cultures; delaying until cultures clear is inappropriate for active infection.

question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis has a 1.5 cm left-sided valvular vegetation on TEE and has had an embolic stroke despite antibiotics. Based on the slides, which management step is most strongly indicated?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: Large vegetations (>1 cm) with recurrent embolization despite antibiotics are listed as indications for surgical intervention.

options.text: Continue antibiotics only for six weeks
options.rationale: Wrong: Recurrent embolization and large vegetation despite therapy prompt surgical evaluation rather than antibiotics alone.
Wrong: Oral bacteriostatic therapy is inappropriate for large vegetations and embolic complications; bactericidal IV therapy and surgery are indicated.
Wrong: Anticoagulation in the setting of septic emboli and IE is not the primary management and may be harmful; surgery is prioritized.
Wrong: Percutaneous aspiration is not described in the slides as standard management; surgical removal is the indicated approach for large, embolizing vegetations.

question: Which laboratory abnormalities are described as nonspecific supportive findings in infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides list elevated ESR/CRP and normochromic normocytic anemia among nonspecific supportive lab findings.
Wrong: Eosinophilia and hypercalcemia are not listed as typical lab findings in IE in the slides.
Wrong: Thrombocytopenia may occur in some staphylococcal infections; isolated thrombocytosis is not emphasized as a typical finding.
Wrong: Low ESR is not characteristic; the slides describe elevated acute phase reactants and variable WBC counts.
Wrong: Hypocomplementemia, not high complement, is mentioned among immune-related nonspecific findings in some patients.

question: A 9-year-old with ARF has migratory arthritis and elevated ASO titers. According to the slides, what is the role of bedrest in management?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Acute Rheumatic Fever

options.text: Bedrest until temperature and ECG normalize
options.rationale: Correct: The slides recommend bedrest and continuation of treatment until temperature normalizes and ECG returns to normal.
Wrong: The slides advise bedrest during acute illness until clinical and ECG recovery, so encouraging full activity is incorrect.

options.text: Bedrest only for carditis with CHF
options.rationale: Wrong: Bedrest is recommended more broadly during acute ARF until fever and ECG normalize, not only for CHF cases.
Wrong: Prolonged bedrest for a year is not recommended; the slides specify bedrest during the acute phase until clinical improvement.
Wrong: Bedrest is part of general acute management, not limited solely to severe arthritis per the slides.

question: Which of the following is a correct pairing of infective endocarditis organism and recommended targeted therapy from the slides for left-sided native valve disease?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides list ampicillin or PCN G with gentamicin for enterococcal left-sided native valve IE.
Wrong: S. aureus is treated with nafcillin or cefazolin ± gentamicin for MSSA; ceftriaxone monotherapy is not the recommended regimen.
Wrong: HACEK organisms are treated with ceftriaxone or ampicillin per the slides; vancomycin is not the first choice.
Wrong: Fungal IE requires antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B and often surgery; penicillin G is ineffective.
Wrong: Pneumococcal IE is treated with PCN G or ampicillin per the slides; nafcillin targets staphylococci, not pneumococcus.

question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis has conduction abnormalities on ECG suggesting an aortic root complication. Which complication listed in the slides is most consistent with new heart block?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides note valvular ring abscess often presents with conduction defects such as AV block and is a surgical indication.
Wrong: Peripheral emboli cause systemic signs but do not explain new conduction defects; ring abscess does.
Wrong: Conjunctival petechiae are peripheral stigmata and would not cause heart block.
Wrong: Roth spots are retinal lesions from emboli and immune phenomena, not causes of conduction abnormalities.
Wrong: Splinter hemorrhages are peripheral embolic signs and do not produce AV conduction defects.

question: Which of the following best describes the natural history progression from acute rheumatic fever to chronic rheumatic heart disease as presented?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.text: Acute pancarditis then chronic valvular lesions
options.rationale: Correct: The slides describe ARF causing pancarditis acutely and chronic valvular lesions (eg, mitral stenosis) developing years later.

options.text: Acute pericarditis resolving without valvular change
options.rationale: Wrong: While pericarditis can occur, the slide emphasizes valvulitis leading to chronic valvular disease rather than isolated pericarditis resolution.

options.text: Immediate calcific aortic stenosis within weeks
options.rationale: Wrong: Chronic valvular calcification and stenosis develop over years (10–20 years), not within weeks.
Wrong: The primary long-term sequelae are valvular lesions; MI is not described as the typical progression.

options.text: Tricuspid stenosis as the dominant outcome
options.rationale: Wrong: Mitral valve disease is most common; tricuspid stenosis is not the dominant chronic outcome per the slides.

question: A 28-year-old IV drug user presents with fever and multiple pulmonary nodular infiltrates on chest x-ray. Based on the lecture content, which type and location of infective endocarditis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: IV drug use commonly causes right-sided IE (tricuspid), and septic pulmonary emboli produce pulmonary nodular infiltrates as noted in the slides.
Wrong: Left-sided IE typically causes systemic emboli and pulmonary edema, not septic pulmonary nodules associated with right-sided disease.
Wrong: Prosthetic valve IE is less specifically linked to IV drug use and pulmonary septic emboli; right-sided native valve IE is more likely.
Wrong: HACEK organisms cause subacute left-sided disease and are not the classic cause of pulmonary septic emboli in IV drug users.
Wrong: Fungal IE can occur but the clinical picture of IV drug use with pulmonary nodules is most consistent with right-sided bacterial IE.

question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis is hemodynamically stable but has a prosthetic pacemaker and positive blood cultures. The slides emphasize device management. What is the recommended action regarding the pacemaker?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.text: Complete removal of all pacemaker hardware
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state pacemaker/defibrillator infections require complete removal of all hardware along with antibiotics.

options.text: Leave hardware and treat with IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong: Retaining infected hardware is contraindicated per the slides; removal is required for cure.

options.text: Replace generator only and retain leads
options.rationale: Wrong: Partial replacement leaving infected leads risks persistent infection; complete hardware removal is recommended.

options.text: Switch to oral antibiotics after 48 hours
options.rationale: Wrong: Device-related IE requires prolonged IV therapy and hardware removal; early switch to oral therapy is inappropriate.
Wrong: Externalization without removal does not eliminate the nidus of infection; slides recommend complete removal.

question: Which of the following is an accurate statement about the timing and organisms of prosthetic valve endocarditis as presented?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.text: Early PVE often involves coagulase-negative staphylococci
options.rationale: Correct: The slides indicate early ( 12 months) is more often due to streptococci and HACEK organisms per the slides; Candida is not the typical late cause.

options.text: Early PVE is most commonly HACEK organisms
options.rationale: Wrong: HACEK organisms are associated with late or subacute infections, not the early postoperative prosthetic infections described.

options.text: Prosthetic valves are rarely infected within first year
options.rationale: Wrong: The slides specifically note early PVE occurs within 12 months and is a recognized risk period.

options.text: Late PVE always presents with negative blood cultures
options.rationale: Wrong: Late PVE can have positive cultures; HACEK organisms may be slow-growing but cultures are often positive with appropriate techniques.

question: A patient with severe mitral regurgitation from rheumatic disease has progressive left ventricular dysfunction and symptoms of heart failure. According to the slides, what is the indicated next step in management?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.rationale: Correct: The slides state that symptomatic MR or declining LVEF are indications for mitral valve repair or replacement.
Wrong: Progressive symptoms or LV dysfunction warrant surgical intervention rather than continued medical therapy alone per the slides.
Wrong: Balloon valvuloplasty is a treatment for mitral stenosis, not for severe MR which typically requires repair or replacement.
Wrong: Anticoagulation may be needed for AF, but it does not correct severe MR with LV dysfunction; valve surgery is indicated.
Wrong: TAVR addresses aortic stenosis, not mitral regurgitation; it is not the appropriate intervention here.

question: Which of the following best summarizes the recommended empiric antibiotic approach when infective endocarditis is suspected but cultures are pending, according to the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides recommend empiric vancomycin with or without an aminoglycoside (eg, gentamicin) after obtaining cultures.
Wrong: Empiric therapy for suspected IE should be IV and cover MRSA; oral amoxicillin is inadequate.
Wrong: Amphotericin B is for fungal IE and is not the empiric choice for typical bacterial IE per the slides.
Wrong: Antibiotics should be started after obtaining blood cultures; waiting for TEE may delay necessary therapy in unstable patients.
Wrong: Oral doxycycline is not an appropriate empiric regimen for suspected IE; IV bactericidal therapy is recommended.

question: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis has three sets of blood cultures drawn 30 minutes apart and all are negative, but TEE shows a 1.2 cm vegetation. According to the slides, which organism group might be considered given culture-negative endocarditis and slow growth?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides note HACEK organisms are fastidious, slow-growing causes of endocarditis that can yield delayed or initially negative cultures.
Wrong: S. aureus typically grows readily in cultures and is not a classic cause of culture-negative, slow-growing IE.
Wrong: Viridans streptococci usually grow in cultures; HACEK organisms are specifically noted for slow growth.
Wrong: Fungal organisms can be culture-negative initially but the slides specifically highlight HACEK as fastidious bacteria causing delayed growth.
Wrong: Enterococci typically grow in cultures and are not the prototypical fastidious organisms described as culture-negative in the slides.

question: Which of the following is a correct statement about the duration of therapy for infective endocarditis as presented in the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.rationale: Correct: The slides indicate typical treatment durations are usually 4–6 weeks depending on organism and severity.

options.text: All IE treated for exactly two weeks
options.rationale: Wrong: Some indolent strains may be treated for 2 weeks in specific regimens, but many require 4–6 weeks; a blanket two-week rule is incorrect.

options.text: Therapy duration is one week for staphylococci
options.rationale: Wrong: Aggressive organisms like S. aureus often require longer therapy (eg, 6 weeks), not one week.
Wrong: Oral therapy is not routinely used to shorten duration; IV bactericidal therapy for the recommended duration is standard per the slides.

options.text: Duration depends only on patient age
options.rationale: Wrong: Duration depends on organism virulence and prosthetic involvement, not solely on age.

question: A patient with acute rheumatic fever has severe mitral stenosis developing 15 years after the initial illness. According to the slides, which intervention is most appropriate when symptoms of mitral stenosis become limiting?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Rheumatic Heart Disease

options.text: Balloon mitral valvuloplasty or valve replacement
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state severe mitral stenosis is mechanical disease requiring balloon valvuloplasty or surgical replacement when symptomatic.
Wrong: Aspirin treats acute ARF inflammation but does not correct chronic mechanical MS; valvuloplasty or replacement is needed for severe symptomatic disease.
Wrong: Aortic valve replacement addresses aortic disease, not mitral stenosis; mitral-specific interventions are indicated.
Wrong: PCI treats coronary artery disease and is unrelated to mechanical mitral stenosis management.
Wrong: Anticoagulation may be needed for AF but does not relieve symptomatic mitral stenosis; mechanical intervention is required.

question: Which of the following peripheral signs is described in the slides as a painless erythematous lesion on palms or soles associated with infective endocarditis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.text: Janeway lesions on palms or soles
options.rationale: Correct: Janeway lesions are macular, nonpainful erythematous lesions on palms and soles and are classic for IE per the slides.
Wrong: Osler nodes are painful violaceous nodules on fingers and toes, not painless palmar/plantar lesions.
Wrong: Splinter hemorrhages are linear nail-bed lesions, not macular palmar/plantar erythema.
Wrong: Roth spots are retinal hemorrhagic lesions, not palmar or plantar macules.
Wrong: Conjunctival petechiae are ocular findings and not the painless palmar/plantar lesions described as Janeway lesions.

question: Which of the following best characterizes the recommended approach to home therapy for infective endocarditis as described in the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiology, risk factors, presentation, evaluation and management of Infectious Endocarditis

options.text: Individualize based on organism and severity
options.rationale: Correct: The slides state decisions about oral or home therapy should be individualized according to organism ID, sensitivities, and severity.

options.text: All patients should complete therapy inpatient
options.rationale: Wrong: The slides allow for individualized home therapy in select cases; not all patients must remain inpatient.
Wrong: Home therapy is not universally contraindicated; the slides suggest individualization.

options.text: Oral antibiotics are preferred for all
options.rationale: Wrong: Oral antibiotics are not routinely preferred; IV bactericidal therapy is standard and oral therapy is considered case-by-case.
Wrong: Home therapy would still require close monitoring and follow-up; the slides emphasize individualized decisions, not no follow-up.
